title: Oedipus Rex
author: Sophocles
openingText: My children, latest born to Cadmus old, why sit ye here as suppliants, in your hands branches of olive filleted with wool? What means this reek of incense everywhere, and everywhere laments and litanies? Children, it were not meet that I should learn from others, and am hither come, myself, I Oedipus, your world-renowned king. Ho! aged sire, whose venerable locks proclaim thee spokesman of this company, explain your mood and purport. Is it dread of ill that moves you or a boon ye crave? My zeal in your behalf ye cannot doubt; ruthless indeed were I and obdurate if such petitioners as you I spurned.
about:
Thebes is dying. Plague has rotted the harvest, the livestock, the women in childbirth. King Oedipus — who once saved this city by solving the Sphinx's riddle — vows to find the source of the pollution and drive it out. The oracle is clear: find the murderer of the old king Laius. Oedipus begins his investigation. He does not stop when the clues start pointing toward himself.

Sophocles wrote this play for an audience who already knew the ending. That is the point. We watch a brilliant, courageous man deploy every virtue — intelligence, persistence, the refusal to look away — and we see those same virtues tighten the trap. This is the foundational text of Western tragedy, the play that gave us the concept of tragic irony. It is also, at its core, a detective story in which the detective is the murderer.

angleCards.title: The virtues that destroy him.
angleCards.text: Oedipus is not brought down by weakness. He is too smart, too honest, too relentless. Every quality that made him a good king — and a good detective — becomes the instrument of his destruction. Track what his virtues cost him.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a study in how a man's greatest strengths can become the mechanism of his own ruin.

angleCards.title: Tragic irony and the audience's knowledge.
angleCards.text: Sophocles performed this for an audience who already knew the story. Every hopeful line lands differently when you know where it leads. Notice which moments the audience understands and Oedipus does not — and what Sophocles does with that gap.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how dramatic irony works — how knowing the ending changes what every line means, and why Sophocles built the whole play on that gap.

angleCards.title: Fate versus self-determination.
angleCards.text: The oracle told Oedipus's parents what he would do. Oedipus's parents acted to prevent it — and caused it. Oedipus acted to escape it — and fulfilled it. Ask whether anyone in this play could have chosen differently, or whether choice itself is the mechanism the gods use.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the question of whether fate and free will are actually opposites — or whether the choices characters make are exactly what fate required.

angleCards.title: Pollution and the city.
angleCards.text: The Greek concept of miasma — ritual pollution that spreads from a guilty person outward into the land itself — is not metaphor here. It is the operating premise. The city is sick because something unclean is at its centre. Ask what this logic demands of a king.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the Greek idea of pollution — miasma — and what it means that a king's hidden guilt can poison an entire city.

cast.name: Oedipus
cast.description: Brilliant, fearless, and impatient. He solved the Sphinx's riddle and won a city and a queen. Now he faces another riddle — and insists on solving it regardless of where the answer leads.

cast.name: Iocasta
cast.description: Wife of Oedipus and, before him, of Laius. She is pragmatic and politically shrewd, inclined to dismiss prophecy as superstition. She begins urging Oedipus to stop asking questions before he does.

cast.name: Creon
cast.description: Oedipus's brother-in-law and second-in-command. He brings back Apollo's oracle and bears the brunt of Oedipus's suspicion when the investigation starts to implicate him.

cast.name: Tiresias
cast.description: The only man in Thebes who already knows the answer. He refuses to speak. When Oedipus forces the truth from him, no one believes it — including Oedipus.

cast.name: Priest of Zeus
cast.description: He opens the play at the altar steps, speaking for the suffering citizens of Thebes. His appeal to Oedipus sets the investigation in motion.

cast.name: Chorus of Theban Elders
cast.description: The elders of Thebes who comment, grieve, and interpret between scenes. They resist the truth longest — because accepting it means accepting what their king is.
